paragraphs: Distributed learning divides computation among workers, but keeping every worker busy does not necessarily use resources efficiently. Devices can have different and unpredictable completion times. A greedy asynchronous strategy can therefore spend substantially more computation than needed, even though its purpose is to accelerate training.

ATA addresses this allocation problem without assuming that worker timing distributions are known beforehand. It adapts task assignments to heterogeneous, random computation times. The motivating idea is that an informed allocation would give more work to faster workers; ATA seeks the benefits of that allocation while learning how workers behave.

The theoretical analysis shows that ATA identifies the optimal allocation and performs comparably to methods that already know computation times. Experiments also report significant resource savings relative to greedy allocation. The abstract further identifies how severe the problem can become: the greedy approach can be arbitrarily expensive depending on the worker count. The contribution connects training speed with resource efficiency, rather than treating worker utilization alone as sufficient.
icml-2025-ata-adaptive-task-allocation-f.tldr: ATA learns how to allocate distributed training tasks efficiently when worker computation times are heterogeneous and initially unknown.

paragraphs: A privacy-preserving algorithm can have implementation flaws that undermine its intended protection. Empirical auditing examines the behavior of an implemented mechanism to help catch some of these flaws. Existing approaches face a trade-off: they may require repeated executions of a learning algorithm, or produce privacy estimates that are less tight than they could be.

This paper introduces an audit that requires only one execution of the target mechanism. It obtains useful auditing information from randomness in the examples included in the input dataset. That makes the procedure computationally efficient while retaining the aim of assessing the mechanism’s empirical privacy.

The main analytical contribution uses the mechanism’s hypothesized f-differential privacy curve to obtain tighter estimates. This curve provides a more detailed privacy description than the traditional epsilon and delta parameters used in the comparison. The authors demonstrate tighter empirical estimates with their procedure and analysis. The result strengthens what a single-run audit can reveal about privacy behavior, while its role remains empirical assessment capable of catching some implementation problems.
icml-2025-auditing-f-differential-privac.tldr: A single-run privacy audit uses a hypothesized f-DP curve to produce tighter empirical privacy estimates.

paragraphs: An LLM can spend additional computation trying to repair a flawed code solution. AuPair makes those attempts more useful by changing the repair example supplied to the model on each attempt. It uses in-context learning, so the repair strategy operates at inference time without requiring model fine-tuning.

The method synthesizes and selects an ordered collection of examples pairing an incorrect solution with its subsequent fix. For a budget of N model calls, it uses N such pairs, supplying one pair per call to produce N repaired candidates. It then returns the highest-scoring candidate. Selection aims to make the examples complementary and useful, with the intuition that different repair demonstrations encourage diverse proposed fixes.

The authors evaluate the approach using five LLMs and seven competitive programming datasets. They report significant improvements over best-of-N and self-repair, strong generalization across datasets and models, and stronger scaling as inference budgets increase. These findings suggest that the choice of repair demonstrations can materially affect how much benefit additional model calls provide.
icml-2025-aupair-golden-example-pairs-fo.tldr: AuPair selects complementary examples of code fixes to improve the diversity and effectiveness of repeated LLM repair attempts.

paragraphs: Training autonomous agents requires environments where they can interact, navigate, and solve problems. Fast two-dimensional environments leave out challenges associated with three-dimensional space, while richer 3D environments can be expensive to run. Customization and support for multiple interacting agents introduce further requirements for a useful research platform.

Craftium provides a platform for building customizable 3D environments for both individual agents and groups of agents. The paper demonstrates a range of settings, including focused tasks, large worlds containing different creatures and biomes, and procedural generators whose tasks can be customized. This range matters because environment tools need to accommodate different research questions and levels of complexity.

Benchmarking shows lower computational costs than alternatives offering similar richness. In particular, the authors report a throughput advantage of more than 2,000 steps per second over Minecraft-based frameworks. The contribution is an environment-building platform that combines rich 3D interaction with efficient execution, making flexibility and simulation speed available within the same tool.
icml-2025-craftium-bridging-flexibility-.tldr: Craftium provides customizable 3D environments for single and multiple agents while reducing simulation costs relative to similarly rich alternatives.

paragraphs: Methods for training certifiably robust neural networks are difficult to compare when their evaluations use different schedules, certification procedures, or levels of hyperparameter tuning. CTBench addresses this problem with a unified library and benchmark that evaluates algorithms under fair conditions and systematically tunes their settings.

Under this evaluation, almost all included algorithms exceed their previously reported performance by amounts comparable to algorithmic improvements. These results establish new state-of-the-art performance, while also substantially reducing the apparent advantage of recent methods once older baselines receive comparable schedules, certification methods, and tuning. The findings show how evaluation choices affect conclusions about progress.

CTBench also supports observations about certified models: their loss surfaces are less fragmented, they share many mistakes, and their activations are sparser. The authors identify carefully reducing regularization as crucial, particularly for larger certification radii. They additionally find that certified training has the potential to improve generalization outside the training distribution. Together, these results make the benchmark useful for both comparison and investigation of how certified training behaves.
icml-2025-ctbench-a-library-and-benchmar.tldr: CTBench shows that fair evaluation and thorough tuning substantially improve certified-training results and narrow the reported advantages of newer algorithms.

paragraphs: Diffusion models on curved spaces must respect the geometry of the space where samples live. For symmetric manifolds such as spheres, tori, and certain matrix groups, existing approaches often rely on heat kernels that lack closed-form expressions. Computing with these kernels can require many gradient evaluations or arithmetic costs that grow exponentially with dimension.

The proposed framework avoids heat-kernel computations by using a diffusion with spatially varying covariance and a projection of Euclidean Brownian motion. The authors derive a training objective through Ito’s Lemma. For dimension d, each training step requires O(1) gradient evaluations and O(d^1.19) arithmetic operations, bringing its computational demands closer to those of diffusion in Euclidean space.

Symmetries of the manifold provide an average-case Lipschitz condition that supports accurate, efficient sampling. Experiments on synthetic data on the torus, special orthogonal group, and unitary group show faster training and improved sample quality relative to prior methods. The stated framework covers symmetric manifolds, and the empirical results concern the listed geometric settings.
icml-2025-efficient-diffusion-models-for.tldr: A geometry-aware diffusion framework avoids expensive heat-kernel calculations and improves training efficiency on symmetric manifolds.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction equips a neural network with sets of possible answers and finite-sample guarantees. Adversarial changes to inputs can invalidate ordinary conformal guarantees. Existing robust alternatives address this issue, but at large scales they can produce overly large prediction sets or require too much computation for practical deployment.

The paper introduces lip-rcp, which uses networks with bounded sensitivity to input changes to estimate robust prediction sets precisely and efficiently. Combined with a 1-Lipschitz robust network, the method achieves better set sizes and computational efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art approaches in medium- and large-scale settings, including ImageNet. The network condition is part of the stated result.

The authors also examine ordinary conformal prediction under attack. They derive worst-case coverage bounds that apply simultaneously across all adversarial attack levels. Their method makes this second approach as efficient as ordinary conformal prediction while adding robustness guarantees. The work therefore addresses both constructing robust sets and understanding how much coverage ordinary sets retain under adversarial perturbations.
icml-2025-efficient-robust-conformal-pre.tldr: Lip-rcp uses Lipschitz-bounded networks to make robust conformal prediction sets smaller and more computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a delayed improvement in generalization: a model fits its training data well before its test accuracy suddenly rises. This paper shows that the phenomenon can occur outside neural networks and without gradient-descent-based optimization. Its setting is modular arithmetic learned using Recursive Feature Machines, an iterative method that learns task-specific features through the Average Gradient Outer Product.

When combined with kernel machines, these iterations produce a rapid transition from near-zero test accuracy to perfect accuracy. Training loss remains zero, and test loss initially stays constant, so those losses do not reveal the approaching transition. The authors instead trace it to the gradual development of block-circulant features.

Neural networks solving the same type of arithmetic also learn block-circulant features. The paper supplies theoretical evidence that Recursive Feature Machines use them to implement the Fourier Multiplication Algorithm. The findings demonstrate that learning suitable features alone can produce this form of emergence. They also provide further evidence for the Average Gradient Outer Product as a mechanism relevant to feature learning in neural networks.
icml-2025-emergence-in-non-neural-models.tldr: Recursive Feature Machines exhibit grokking on modular arithmetic, showing that delayed generalization can emerge from feature learning outside neural networks.

paragraphs: A foundation model for time series needs a way to represent real-valued sequences as discrete tokens. WaveToken approaches this through wavelets, which represent frequency information localized in time. This gives the model a vocabulary for both coarse patterns and fine details rather than treating all temporal structure at one level.

The method scales and decomposes the input series, then thresholds and quantizes the resulting wavelet coefficients. An autoregressive model is pretrained to predict coefficients over the future forecast horizon. The purpose of this representation is to make complex temporal structure compact and easier for the model to learn.

Across a benchmark of 42 datasets covering in-domain and zero-shot settings, WaveToken matches or exceeds recently proposed forecasting foundation models with a vocabulary of 1,024 tokens. It is also competitive with modern models trained specifically for each dataset and achieves the best average rank on three complementary metrics. The reported results include successful handling of trends, sparse spikes, and changing frequencies, supporting the value of tokenization that separates temporal structures at different scales.
icml-2025-enhancing-foundation-models-fo.tldr: WaveToken represents time series with wavelet-based tokens, achieving strong forecasting and generalization results with a compact vocabulary.

paragraphs: A model reasoning about a physical scene may not have an updated scan whenever something changes. Hypo3D evaluates whether models can instead use a description of a change to imagine the revised scene and answer questions about it. This addresses the cost of frequently acquiring fresh scene data, an assumption built into existing 3D reasoning benchmarks.

The benchmark contains 7,727 described context changes across 700 indoor scenes, producing 14,885 question-answer pairs. It establishes an anchor-based world frame so directional language in both changes and questions refers consistently to the same global frame. This makes spatial references a defined part of the task.

Experiments find that state-of-the-art foundation models struggle with these hypothetical scenes and fall substantially behind humans. Movement changes and directional reasoning are particularly difficult. Models also often change their answers when the described scene change is irrelevant to the question. The benchmark therefore examines both whether models update spatial conclusions when needed and whether they preserve conclusions that a change should leave unaffected.
icml-2025-hypo3d-exploring-hypothetical-.tldr: Hypo3D reveals difficulties in reasoning about described changes to 3D scenes, including unnecessary answer changes when the relevant facts stay the same.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparison models describe outcomes of comparisons between agents. This paper asks whether observed comparisons are compatible with a generalized Thurstone model for a specified choice function. That question comes before estimating a model’s parameters: it tests whether the proposed model class is an appropriate description of the data.

The authors define a separation distance between general comparison models and the chosen Thurstone class. They derive upper and lower bounds on how far an alternative must be from that class for testing to be possible. These bounds depend on the observation graph, which records which pairs are compared. When every pair is observed, the critical threshold scales as the inverse square root of nk, with n agents and k comparisons per pair.

The framework includes a test based on this distance, confidence intervals, and time-uniform control of both types of testing error using reverse martingales. Information-theoretic arguments establish minimax lower bounds. Synthetic and real-world experiments validate the results, linking the theoretical testing limits to practical comparison data.
icml-2025-hypothesis-testing-for-general.tldr: The paper develops tests and statistical limits for determining whether pairwise comparisons fit a specified generalized Thurstone model.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks use relationships between entities to improve predictions, but the relevant relationships may be unknown. In that case, graph structure learning infers them alongside the network’s other parameters. Because the graph is latent, there are no directly observed graphs to tell the model whether its inferred relationships are correct.

The paper demonstrates that minimizing a loss for point predictions does not guarantee recovery of either the latent relational information or its uncertainty. A training objective can therefore be useful for predicting the target without guaranteeing that the graph representation is learned properly. This distinction matters when the learned relationships themselves are part of the intended output.

The authors prove that suitable losses on stochastic model outputs can support both objectives simultaneously: learning the unknown distribution over graphs and achieving optimal target predictions. They then propose a sampling-based method for this joint task. Empirical results support the theoretical claims and the method’s effectiveness. The contribution identifies a route to learning predictive behavior and uncertainty about the underlying relationships together.
icml-2025-learning-latent-graph-structur.tldr: Suitable losses on stochastic outputs can jointly learn latent graph uncertainty and optimal predictions, where point-prediction losses provide no such guarantee.

paragraphs: Many real-world time series reflect nonlinear dynamics, yet successful deep forecasting systems do not always model those dynamics explicitly. DeepEDM combines a dynamical-systems approach with a neural network, aiming to connect the representation used for prediction with the process governing how the series evolves.

The framework is inspired by empirical dynamic modeling and grounded in Takens’ theorem. It starts from time-delayed embeddings, which assemble observations from different times, and learns a latent representation of them. Kernel regression then approximates the underlying dynamics in that representation. An efficient softmax-attention implementation supports this computation and prediction of future time steps.

The authors evaluate DeepEDM on synthetic nonlinear dynamical systems and real-world time series from multiple domains. They report robustness to input noise and better forecasting accuracy than state-of-the-art methods in their experiments. The results support combining learned representations with explicit modeling of temporal dynamics. The contribution is the integration of these components into a forecasting framework, rather than relying on a neural representation alone to capture the evolution implicitly.
icml-2025-lets-forecast-learning-embedol.tldr: DeepEDM combines learned time-delay representations with nonlinear dynamics modeling to improve forecasting accuracy and robustness to input noise.

paragraphs: Learning to defer means deciding which expert should handle each input while balancing accuracy against computational cost. Training usually relies on surrogate losses that are easier to optimize than the routing objective itself. This paper studies whether minimizing those surrogates gives reliable guarantees for the intended deferral decisions.

The authors distinguish two settings: jointly learning a predictor and a deferral function, and learning the deferral function with an expert held fixed. For joint learning, they introduce a family of losses with realizable H-consistency and prove H-consistency for one selected member. These guarantees concern the relationship between surrogate optimization and deferral performance within a specified hypothesis class.

For two-stage learning, the proposed losses provide realizable H-consistency, H-consistency bounds, and Bayes-consistency with two experts. The multiple-expert extension requires natural assumptions, and low-noise assumptions yield stronger guarantees in both learning settings. The paper also presents efficient algorithms and experimental comparisons with existing baselines. Its central contribution is a set of differentiated guarantees for practical routing objectives, with the conditions and strength depending on the learning scenario.
icml-2025-mastering-multiple-expert-rout.tldr: New surrogate losses provide theoretical guarantees for routing inputs among experts while balancing prediction accuracy and computational cost.

paragraphs: Model merging combines task-specific model weights into one model that serves several tasks. The merged model can still perform substantially worse than the separate specialists. This paper investigates task matrices, the weight changes made to a pretrained model, to understand which properties support effective merging.

The authors find a strong correlation between performance gains over the pretrained model and alignment between singular components of task-specific and merged matrices. They use this observation to design an isotropic merging framework that flattens the singular-value spectrum. The framework also incorporates both shared subspaces and subspaces specific to individual tasks, further improving alignment and performance.

The proposed method reduces the performance gap and achieves state-of-the-art results on vision and language tasks across several task collections and model scales. It does so without additional training. The contribution ties an observed structural relationship in weight updates to a concrete merging procedure. The correlation motivates the design, while the reported evaluations provide evidence that preserving and balancing these matrix components improves the resulting multitask model.
icml-2025-no-task-left-behind-isotropic-.tldr: An isotropic merging method balances shared and task-specific weight-update components to improve multitask performance without additional training.

paragraphs: A model’s correct answers on a benchmark are often treated as evidence that it understands the tested concepts. This paper develops a formal framework for examining that inference, especially when the benchmark was also designed to test people. The issue is whether the same observed answers justify the same interpretation of ability.

Within the framework, those benchmarks are valid tests only if model misunderstandings mirror human misunderstandings. The authors call apparent success based on answers incompatible with any human interpretation of a concept potemkin understanding. This makes the coherence of answers across uses of a concept central to assessing what benchmark success actually establishes.

The paper introduces two measurement procedures: a purpose-built benchmark spanning three domains and a general method that gives a lower bound on the prevalence of these failures. The authors find them widespread across the examined models, tasks, and domains. They interpret the failures as evidence of internal incoherence in concept representations, beyond simply holding an incorrect understanding. The result challenges straightforward human-style interpretations of model benchmark performance.
icml-2025-potemkin-understanding-in-larg.tldr: The paper finds widespread incoherence in LLM concept use that can make correct benchmark answers misleading evidence of human-like understanding.

paragraphs: Ordinary binary classification loss may poorly reflect the goal when classes are imbalanced or different mistakes carry different costs. Measures such as F-beta, Jaccard similarity, AM, and weighted accuracy can better match these needs, but directly optimizing them introduces computational and statistical challenges.

A common strategy estimates class probabilities and then searches for a decision threshold. The paper identifies a gap in such approaches: they are not tailored to restricted hypothesis classes and lack finite-sample guarantees. The authors instead reformulate generalized metric optimization as a generalized cost-sensitive learning problem, making the costs of decisions part of the optimization framework.

This reformulation supports new surrogate losses with H-consistency guarantees and leads to the METRO algorithms. The analysis includes finite-sample generalization bounds, connecting the training approach to performance with a limited dataset. Experimental comparisons demonstrate effectiveness against prior baselines. The contribution is a principled route from the chosen evaluation metric to trainable objectives, with guarantees that account for the hypothesis class used by the learner.
icml-2025-principled-algorithms-for-opti.tldr: METRO converts generalized classification metrics into cost-sensitive learning objectives with hypothesis-class-aware and finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Length generalization asks how sequence predictors perform when the relevant temporal context extends beyond what is available to the learner. This paper makes that comparison explicit through a new performance measure called Asymmetric-Regret. It evaluates the learner against a benchmark predictor that can use a longer context.

The asymmetry is central to the formulation: the learner and its comparator do not receive the same amount of history. The metric therefore measures performance against a predictor with a context advantage. This gives a precise way to study length generalization rather than evaluating only against a benchmark restricted to the learner’s own context length.

The authors investigate this objective using spectral filtering and present a gradient-based learning algorithm with a provable length-generalization result for linear dynamical systems. That system class is the stated scope of the theoretical guarantee. They also provide proof-of-concept experiments consistent with the theory. The contribution combines a formal comparison criterion with an algorithmic result, giving a theoretical foundation for studying prediction with unequal context lengths.
icml-2025-provable-length-generalization.tldr: A spectral-filtering algorithm provably generalizes in context length for linear dynamical systems under a new asymmetric regret measure.

paragraphs: Bongard Problems test abstract visual reasoning by requiring a solver to discover concepts across images and express the relevant distinction verbally. This paper uses them to investigate whether multimodal language models can connect visual evidence with abstract concepts across different kinds of imagery.

The authors develop several solution strategies suited to these models and test four proprietary and four open-access models. The evaluation covers three datasets containing both synthetic and real-world images. Although models achieve some success on the real-world datasets, they struggle with classical synthetic Bongard Problems. That difference raises a question about whether unfamiliar image style or reasoning difficulty drives the failures.

To investigate, the authors introduce Bongard-RWR, which expresses concepts from synthetic problems using real-world images. Their findings suggest that the weakness on classical problems stems from general abstract visual reasoning limitations rather than domain specificity. The new dataset helps separate a problem’s visual presentation from its underlying concept, strengthening the investigation of what the models find difficult without making the explanation certain.
icml-2025-reasoning-limitations-of-multi.tldr: Bongard evaluations suggest that multimodal models’ struggles reflect general abstract visual reasoning limitations rather than merely unfamiliar synthetic imagery.

paragraphs: Learning a controller from an unknown system is harder when the goal describes behavior over time rather than a single immediate outcome. This paper studies goals written in linear temporal logic, assuming the unknown system is a Markov decision process with finitely many states and actions.

The central technical result is a regret-free online learning algorithm for infinite-horizon reach-avoid problems. The authors show that general temporal-logic controller synthesis can be reduced to this form once the system’s graph structure is known. They also provide a separate procedure for learning that graph, which assumes knowledge of a minimum transition probability.

The resulting controller-learning approach provides sharp bounds on distance from optimal behavior after a finite number of episodes. This improves on earlier synthesis algorithms whose guarantees describe only eventual behavior and do not characterize performance during learning. The contribution therefore concerns both learning under unknown dynamics and quantifying progress before the asymptotic regime, with graph knowledge or the stated graph-learning assumption playing a distinct role in handling general specifications.
icml-2025-regret-free-reinforcement-lear.tldr: The paper gives regret-free learning for temporal-logic control with finite-episode guarantees under a finite-state, finite-action MDP formulation.

paragraphs: Transformer layers use the residual stream to store features and access information produced elsewhere in the network. This paper changes that shared memory mechanism. The Residual Matrix Transformer replaces the usual residual stream with an outer-product memory matrix, altering how layers retrieve and store information.

The architectural change allows the residual stream’s size to scale independently of computation and parameter count. The authors report that increasing this memory capacity improves performance. This makes the representation carried between layers a separate design dimension, rather than tying its growth directly to increases in overall model size or computation.

In the reported comparisons, the Residual Matrix Transformer reaches the same loss as a transformer with 58% fewer FLOPs, 25% fewer parameters, and 41% fewer training tokens. It also performs better on downstream evaluations. The theoretical analysis supports more efficient scaling of the residual stream and improved variance propagation properties. Together, the empirical and theoretical results suggest that changing how intermediate information is stored can improve the efficiency of transformer computation.
icml-2025-residual-matrix-transformers-s.tldr: Residual Matrix Transformers replace the residual stream with matrix memory, enabling more efficient scaling and improved reported performance.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent distributes learning across workers without requiring their computations to finish together. However, workers can differ greatly in speed, and those speeds can change over time. The paper identifies these variations as a source of suboptimal training time and inefficient scaling in existing asynchronous methods.

Ringmaster ASGD is a new asynchronous method designed for this setting. Its central result is a theoretical guarantee of optimal time complexity even with arbitrarily heterogeneous and dynamically fluctuating worker computation times. The guarantee addresses both persistent differences among workers and changes in their timing during execution.

Optimality here means that the method meets the theoretical lower bounds for time complexity in the analyzed scenarios. The authors present it as the first asynchronous SGD method to achieve that result, closing the gap left by previously proposed variants. This matters because distributing more computation across workers does not by itself establish that training finishes as quickly as theoretically possible. The contribution supplies that time-based guarantee for a demanding worker-timing setting.
icml-2025-ringmaster-asgd-the-first-asyn.tldr: Ringmaster ASGD achieves theoretically optimal time complexity despite arbitrary differences and fluctuations in worker computation times.

paragraphs: Scaffold addresses differences among clients’ datasets in federated learning by using control variates to counter client drift. Its deterministic convergence behavior is well understood, but stochastic gradient updates introduce additional randomness. This paper develops a new analysis of how that randomness affects the algorithm’s performance.

The authors show that the global model parameters and control variates together form a Markov chain that approaches a stationary distribution in Wasserstein distance. This provides a way to analyze the evolving random training state. Using that result, they prove linear speed-up with the number of clients, up to higher-order terms in the step size.

The qualification is consequential: the analysis also identifies a higher-order bias, similar to one in FedAvg, that does not shrink when more clients participate. Increasing client count therefore improves the leading behavior without removing this residual bias. The paper clarifies both the benefit of additional clients and a remaining obstacle in stochastic federated optimization, pointing toward algorithmic improvements beyond simply scaling participation.
icml-2025-scaffold-with-stochastic-gradi.tldr: A new Scaffold analysis proves linear client speed-up up to higher-order step-size terms while identifying a bias that more clients do not remove.

paragraphs: Federated recommenders let devices collaborate in training, but transferring full embedding models and updates can overwhelm limited bandwidth and computation. Individual users change only a sparse portion of these embeddings. Exploiting that sparsity can save resources, yet revealing which entries a user accesses can expose the indices of items they rated.

SecEmb combines private embedding retrieval with secure update aggregation. Devices download the embeddings relevant to them, and the server aggregates their updates. The protocol is lossless and is designed so the server learns no information about rated-item indices or individual updates beyond the aggregated model. Protecting both stages is central to making sparse communication compatible with the stated privacy goal.

Empirical results show reductions of up to 90 times in both download and upload communication, and up to 70 times in device-side computation time compared with secure federated recommendation protocols. The authors also report utility advantages over lossy compression methods. These are reported maximum improvements, supporting the potential of secure sparse processing without implying the same savings in every setting.
icml-2025-secemb-sparsity-aware-secure-f.tldr: SecEmb reduces federated recommendation costs through lossless sparse embedding transfers while protecting rated-item indices and individual updates.

paragraphs: Conservation laws identify quantities that remain unchanged during training dynamics. Although such laws are understood for some shallow linear and ReLU networks, their role in more practical architectures is less developed. This paper studies them through the building blocks used in residual networks and transformers.

The authors show that shallow linear and ReLU blocks, including versions with convolution, have the known conservation laws and no additional ones. They fully characterize the laws for a single attention layer. They also show that adding a skip connection to a block leaves its conservation laws the same as those of the corresponding block without that connection.

The paper then considers laws involving only a subset of parameters, such as those within consecutive layers, a residual block, or an attention layer. It shows that characterizing these laws can be reduced to studying the associated block in isolation. Finally, it examines how principles established for continuous gradient flow persist under discrete optimization, particularly SGD. This connects modular architectural analysis with the distinction between continuous training theory and discrete updates.
icml-2025-transformative-or-conservative.tldr: The paper characterizes conservation laws in neural-network building blocks and shows how local parameter laws can be studied in isolation.
